There were days in Vietnam that seemed like a miracle. I remember one afternoon while my platoon was conducting as sweep across a dry rice paddy when we came under heavy automatic fire from the treeline to our front. You can hear them from about five feet and the closer they are the louder the "snap." North Vietnamese soldiers always targeted the commander and his radio operator and so the "snaps" around me in the assault were like strings of firecrackers going off. After everyone had been medivaced, the four of us walked 10 miles back to the battalion compound that night. The next day, I received 17 Marine replacements. I lost track at how many Marines in my platoon were killed and wounded that year. A lot at first and almost none at the end.

I can't remember all of the names who were killed and wounded. Some were killed and wounded on the first day. And after 50 years I've forgotten a lot of the names of those who did make it back to their friends and families. But I still see their faces. Every time I was in DC on business, I'd have the taxi stop at the Vietnam Memorial and wait.
